title: Speeders just got lucky: the new Chevy police Silverado is NOT electric
content:
Chevrolet
speed limit
Jo Borrás
| Nov 1 2026 - 7:57 am PT
Say what you will about America’s police forces,
but they are loyal
– often to each other,
and always to their preferred brand of pursuit vehicle
. And if the thin blue line of Chevy faithful won’t embrace the 750 hp electric Silverado because it’s powered by batteries, that can really only be called a win for the scofflaws they’re pursuing.
A new 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 9C1 police pursuit vehicle (PPV) was on display in the GM Fleet booth at the Orange County Convention Center this past week, where the new half-ton was featured fitted a new, 402 hp version of the venerable 5.7 small-block Chevy V8 sending 428 lb-ft of torque to both axles through a 10-speed automatic transmission. The 9C1 also features an available 2″ lift kit that retains the truck’s pursuit rating, up to 9,300 lbs. of towing capacity, and an available driver’s side LED spotlight.
If that all sounds somewhat pedestrian, it might be because
Electrek
readers are more familiar with the Silverado EV,
which offers more than 750 hp in WOW mode
and 775 lb-ft of torque at 0 rpm,
along with a pessimistic EPA rating of just 478 miles
– which, hilariously, is about the same “range” as the 16 mpg (combined) gas version, despite the EV packing nearly 350 additional horsepower, the ability to cruise in silence,
and the significantly reduced maintenance and total cost of ownership costs of going electric
Which, I guess, are all reasonably obvious things that nobody actually asked me about –
and certainly nobody with a criminal justice degree and a statistically low LSAT score
, so I’ll get back to talking about the truck, itself.
A massive, 16″ touchscreen display dominates the interior of the PPV, and was also touted as a standard feature (as it across Chevy’s civilian line), though if and how it would integrate with police department software isn’t clear –
and my guess is that enforcement computing will continue to be an upfitter issue

title: I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth
content:
electric trucks
Micah Toll
| Nov 1 2026 - 5:29 am PT
Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.
The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my
original unboxing and testing video
quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.
It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”
My mini-truck from China in its first year, not a scratch on it (yet)
I gave an update
after the first year
, showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.
Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.
So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video
. Trust me, you’ll want to.
Five years of actual work
First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.
Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.
Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.
My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.
Filling the electric truck’s bed with a NESHER L880 electric loader makes for the quietest work site ever
We’ve also made
some improvements
over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.
The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.
But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.
And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).
The truck is more at home on dirt roads or pasture than paved streets
So, what’s actually broken after five years?
Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.
The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.
I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!
Of course, not everything is perfect.
The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.
Florida is a very wet state and the truck has to deal with the rains and the high humidity
The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.
Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the
The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.
One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.
And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.
There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.
It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.
That hydraulic dump bed is one of the best features. Let’s see your F150 do that…
What about all that Chinese steel rusting away?
One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.
To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.
Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.
The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.
A recent photo showing the yellowing of the tail light lenses from daily UV exposure at the lowest latitudes in the US
The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).
We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.
After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.
Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.
Running my NESHER L1400 electric loader in excavator mode and using the truck to move the digging spoils
Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.
You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.
Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.
Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.
Dump bed strikes again!
The real test: What does my dad think?
Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.
And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.
He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.
In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.
It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have
a Kandi electric UTV
, which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.
But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.
My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.
A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.
Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.
Was it really $2,000, and was it worth it?
Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.
Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).
Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.
And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.
So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.
If you aren’t towing a boat with it, then do you really have a truck?
Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.
Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.
It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.
This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.
But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.
I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.
The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.
I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.
Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.
My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.
When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.
Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

title: Honda has dominated motorcycles for decades. Electric bikes are changing that
content:
Electric Motorcycles
Micah Toll
| Nov 1 2026 - 1:17 am PT
Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.
Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.
According to newly released nationwide
sales figures
, Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.
But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.
And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.
While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.
Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.
Vinfast’s bikes are the fastest growing segment in Vietnam
It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.
Vietnam’s transition hasn’t happened in a vacuum, either. Government efforts to reduce urban air pollution, including plans to
restrict gasoline-powered motorcycles in parts of Hanoi
, have helped create an increasingly favorable environment for electric alternatives.
And with companies like VinFast offering an expanding range of electric scooters and motorcycles, riders now have more practical alternatives to gasoline-powered models than ever before.
To be clear, Honda isn’t exactly struggling. Its motorcycle sales are still growing, and the Japanese giant remains the undisputed market leader in Vietnam. But its overall share of the market is shrinking, and its relatively modest growth compared to the exploding electric segment suggests that the market’s center of gravity is beginning to shift.
Vietnam may be just a single example, but it’s an important one of what can happen when electric two-wheelers become viable mainstream alternatives to gasoline motorcycles.
Honda has spent decades perfecting the gasoline motorcycle. The question now is how quickly it can adapt to a market that is increasingly interested in something else.

title: Short-range air defense systems with 360-degree turret installed at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate
content: Amid the heightened concerns about President Donald J. Trump’s safety, the U.S. Secret Service has deployed AN/TWQ-1 Avenger short-range air defense systems (SHORADS) near his residence at the Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida. These systems, manufactured by Boeing, are mounted atop the U.S. Army’s 4X4 military trucks, the Heavy High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle (HMMWV), or Humvees, and were also installed about three miles west of Donald J. Trump International Airport. Mobile missile system The Avenger features a 360-degree rotating turret with two missile pods mounted on a Humvee’s heavy chassis and can fire FIM-92 Stinger missiles . Each launcher has a capacity to hold four of these heat-seeking surface-to-air missiles and operates day and night in all weather conditions. A gunner guards the Avenger from the firing station between the two missile pods and operates the launcher. The crew can also operate the weapon system from a remote control unit up to meters away from the firing line. As operational requirements change, the highly mobile Avenger systems can be repositioned to defend against incoming aerial threats, offering air defense for the maneuver force. The upgraded missile system provides on-the-go defensive protection for troops on the ground and in homeland security operations, countering aerial threats, including drones . These infrared-guided weapons were originally designed to defeat helicopters, aircraft, cruise missiles, and larger unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). They engage aerial targets at low altitudes and are designed to protect specific locations rather than defend an entire region. According to photos shared on online platforms, two such Avengers have been deployed near the Trump International Airport. Counter-UAS to counter hostile drones Besides the Avenger missile systems, North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) and North American Aerospace Defense Command have also deployed Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (UAS) capabilities to support the Secret Service, according to media reports. These counter-drone flyaway kits that are rapidly deployable help to spot, classify, and track UAVs. The systems also have the ability to react to drone threats that are detected using both passive and active sensor systems, such as electro-optical and infrared cameras,  or Ku-band radars. Pulsar-based electronic warfare systems, part of the UAS, can use radio-frequency signals to detect and disrupt hostile drones. They rely on jamming the Global Positioning System (GPS) signals of hostile drones to neutralize or spoof them. However, if the jamming fails, the kits recruit kinetic interceptors or other defeat mechanisms. Earlier this week, soldiers in the United States tested rapidly deployable counter-drone systems . They trained on Trust Automation’s Rapidly Deployable Small-Unmanned Air Defense System, or RD-SUADS, a palletized counter-drone system. RD-SUADS is the air-transportable member of Trust Automation’s Small-Unmanned Air Defense System family, designed to detect, track, identify, and defeat small drones at bases and deployed sites. The company built it to be shipped and set up quickly without relying on local power. ​

title: Sodium vs. lithium: Which battery technology will power the next decade
content: Lithium-ion batteries have become the backbone of electric vehicles and energy storage. But a rival chemistry built around one of the world’s most abundant elements is now becoming more and more viable. Sodium-ion batteries are entering commercial production, with major manufacturers betting they could make energy storage cheaper, more resilient, and less dependent on lithium. In February 2026, China’s CATL and automaker Changan unveiled what they described as the world’s first mass-production passenger vehicle equipped with sodium-ion batteries, with sales planned for the middle of the year. In April, CATL also signed a major agreement to supply 60 gigawatt-hours of sodium-ion batteries to energy storage company Beijing HyperStrong Technology over three years. These developments suggest sodium-ion technology is approaching a new stage. But it still faces a fundamental challenge. Lithium-ion batteries have a considerable head start in energy density, cost, and manufacturing scale. Sodium is abundant, but that doesn’t automatically make better batteries Both technologies work on the same basic principle. During charging and discharging, ions move between a positive electrode (cathode) and a negative electrode (anode), with an electrolyte allowing them to travel between the two. The main difference is the element carrying the charge. Lithium-ion batteries use lithium, while sodium-ion batteries use sodium, which is widely available in seawater and common salts. That abundance could reduce dependence on lithium mining and price fluctuations. Sodium-ion cells can also use aluminum current collectors on both electrodes, potentially reducing their reliance on copper. Some designs avoid lithium, cobalt, and graphite altogether. However, sodium-ion batteries are not automatically free of critical minerals. Certain commercial cathode chemistries still use materials such as nickel and manganese, while their hard-carbon anodes require specialized manufacturing. The supply chain for these components is also much less mature. The International Energy Agency (IEA) notes that sodium-ion battery production remains heavily concentrated in China, despite the potential for more geographically diverse raw-material supplies. Lithium-ion still has the energy-density advantage For electric vehicles, one of the most important measures is energy density. It measures how much energy a battery can store relative to its weight or volume. Here, lithium-ion remains ahead. According to the IEA’s 2026 assessment, the latest sodium-ion cells can reach around 175 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg). By comparison, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells can reach approximately 205 Wh/kg, while nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) batteries can reach around 265 Wh/kg. A less energy-dense battery needs to be larger or heavier to store the same amount of energy. In a vehicle, this can mean less driving range or less space for passengers and cargo. The IEA estimates that an average SUV equipped with sodium-ion batteries could achieve up to 350 kilometers (217 miles) of range, compared with approximately 400-600 kilometers (249–373 miles) for lithium-ion vehicles under average weather conditions. Sodium-ion batteries do have an important advantage in colder environments. The latest cells can retain around 90 percent of their nominal capacity at temperatures as low as -40°C (-40°F), outperforming conventional lithium-ion chemistries, particularly LFP. This could make them useful in cold-weather vehicles and equipment. The competition is shifting toward specific applications Sodium-ion’s strongest near-term opportunity may not be replacing the battery in every electric car. Instead, it could find a place in smaller vehicles, two- and three-wheelers, urban delivery fleets, and stationary energy storage , where weight and volume are sometimes less restrictive. The grid-storage market is particularly interesting. Batteries used to store electricity from solar and wind installations do not need to fit inside a vehicle or maximize driving range. Cost, safety, durability, and reliable performance can matter more than energy density. CATL’s 60 GWh agreement with HyperStrong reflects this opportunity, while its TENER sodium-ion storage system, unveiled in June 2026, points to growing interest in commercial-scale stationary applications. Still, the economics are not settled. Lithium-ion manufacturing has benefited from decades of investment and enormous production volumes. In particular, LFP batteries have become highly cost-competitive, making it difficult for sodium-ion to win simply because sodium is cheaper and more abundant. The IEA says global sodium-ion production in 2025 was less than 1 percent of lithium-ion output. Even announced projects for 2030 represent only a fraction of planned lithium-ion manufacturing capacity. A second battery chemistry, not necessarily a replacement The arrival of sodium-ion batteries is important, but it does not mean lithium-ion is about to lose its dominant position. Lithium-based cells continue to improve, while sodium-ion manufacturers still need to scale production, refine materials, and demonstrate consistent performance. The more likely outcome is a battery industry with multiple chemistries serving different needs. Lithium-ion will remain attractive where range, weight and energy density are priorities. Sodium-ion could become increasingly useful where cold-weather performance, material availability and supply-chain diversification carry greater value. Right now, sodium-ion’s biggest achievement may be giving battery manufacturers another option. And in an industry increasingly shaped by the demand for electric vehicles and grid storage, having more than one viable chemistry could prove just as important as developing a better battery.

title: A Hidden DNA Mechanism Could Explain How 20% of Human Cancers Develop
content:
BAF mutations affect a protein complex that helps regulate gene activity by controlling how DNA is organized and accessed inside cells. Credit: Shutterstock
Researchers have identified an unexpected molecular vulnerability in cancers carrying BAF mutations.
Mutations found in roughly 20% of human cancers may promote tumor growth by changing how DNA is organized inside cells. Researchers have identified a mechanism that allows a regulatory protein to reshape the genome’s three-dimensional structure, altering the activity of genes involved in cell division.
The study, published October 28 in
, links these changes to mutations affecting a protein complex called BAF. Scientists at Weill Cornell Medicine found that blocking a key protein involved in the process reversed the cancer-promoting effects in an animal model, suggesting potential new approaches to treatment.
How Cancer Mutations Change DNA Accessibility
The BAF complex helps control gene activity by regulating how accessible DNA is to other proteins. Its numerous subunits are encoded by more than two dozen genes, and mutations affecting these components occur in cancers of the breast, ovaries, liver, and lymphatic system. Until now, researchers had struggled to explain how such mutations could contribute to malignancy across so many different tissues.
The new findings challenge expectations about how BAF normally functions. “We normally think of the BAF complex as making DNA more accessible, and so we expected its loss to have the opposite effect,” Dr. Meydan said. “Instead, its loss made DNA more accessible to CTCF, with surprisingly far-reaching effects.”
CTCF helps organize DNA into distinct regions by establishing boundaries that influence which genes interact with regulatory elements. These interactions depend partly on how DNA folds and loops within the nucleus. When BAF activity is lost, CTCF gains access to sites that would normally be less accessible, potentially disrupting this intricate organization.
A Shared Mechanism Across Different Cancer Types
“The challenge for us was to find a potential cancer-promoting effect occurring across many different cell types and tissue models,” said Dr. Barisic, who is also the John P. Leonard, M.D./Gwirtzman Family Research Scholar in Lymphoma.
Using several animal and cell models with impaired BAF function, the researchers discovered that CTCF binding increased at thousands of locations throughout the genome. This widespread change reorganized DNA loops and folds, disrupting normal connections between genes and the regulatory regions that control their activity. The resulting shifts in gene expression encouraged faster cell division.
Evidence from mouse experiments and human cancer patient data further supported CTCF’s involvement. In particular, disruptions affecting CTCF were associated with better patient outcomes. The researchers also demonstrated that deleting CTCF in an animal model could reverse the effects of BAF mutations, providing experimental evidence that the protein contributes to the cancer-promoting process.
New Molecular Targets for Cancer Treatment
The team identified two additional protein complexes, PBAF and ISWI, that cooperate with CTCF in driving these changes. Removing either complex also blocked the effects of BAF mutations in experimental models, making all three potential targets for future therapies.
“These findings help us establish a unifying mechanism for one of the most common classes of cancer mutations, and identify CTCF and its partner proteins as candidate therapeutic targets in these cancers,” said study co-corresponding author Dr. Darko Barisic, an assistant professor of cancer biology in medicine and a member of the Sandra and Edward Meyer Cancer Center at Weill Cornell Medicine.
Although the experiments identify promising molecular targets, researchers have not yet established whether blocking these proteins can safely treat cancer in humans. The next challenge is understanding precisely how increased CTCF binding changes the genome and finding ways to interfere with that process.
“We’re currently investigating in more detail what this extensive gain of CTCF does to the genome, and we hope before long to find a drug that blocks this process,” Dr. Barisic said.

title: Can Cats Really Go Vegan? New Research Reveals a Surprising Health Connection
content:
Vegan-fed cats appeared less prone to excess weight in a large survey, suggesting a potential new approach to tackling feline obesity. Credit: Shutterstock
More cat owners are turning to vegan diets for their pets. But is a plant-based diet actually safe for cats?
An online survey of 1,305 cats found that those eating vegan diets had 34% lower odds of being assessed as overweight than those eating conventional meat-based food.
The findings came from caregiver reports of veterinary assessments. All cats had followed their diets for at least one year, with conventional meat-based diets accounting for most (90%) and vegan diets for the remainder (10%).
A Surprising Pattern in Cat Weight
Researchers calculated the difference after accounting for age, sex, neuter status, activity, and feeding practices.
The lower rates of excess weight came despite feeding habits that might have tipped the scales the other way, as Knight explained, “Interestingly, most vegan-fed cats were eating predominantly dry food and were more likely to have food available throughout the day. These are feeding patterns normally associated with increased overweight risk. Yet we still observed lower rates of overweight in this group.”
That observation came from study author Andrew Knight, an adjunct professor at Australia’s Griffith University School of Environment and Science. He emphasized that the relatively small vegan-fed group limited what researchers could conclude.
Weight-Related Health Problems Were Also Lower
Veterinary studies estimate that around 30–60% of domestic cats are overweight or obese. Excess weight is associated with arthritis, diabetes, urinary tract disease, and reduced quality of life, giving researchers a reason to investigate dietary patterns that might help.
Caregivers of vegan-fed cats reported fewer weight-related disorders, with no cases reported for several conditions examined. However, the small number of cats in this group made those results uncertain.
“Carers feeding cats vegan diets also reported lower rates of body weight-related disorders such as osteoarthritis and other musculoskeletal and mobility problems,” Knight said. “However, the relatively small number of vegan-fed cats means these results cannot be considered conclusive.”
Cats fed vegan diets showed lower odds of being classified as overweight compared to those fed a meat-based diet. Credit: Griffith University
What Might Explain the Findings
The survey could not establish why vegan-fed cats appeared less likely to be overweight. Researchers did not analyze the foods themselves, so explanations involving their ingredients or nutritional composition remain possibilities.
Some commercial vegan cat foods may provide more fiber and fewer calories or less fat than comparable meat-based products, potentially supporting weight control. Differences in L-carnitine, a nutrient involved in energy metabolism and maintaining lean body tissue, could also contribute.
The results do not establish that avoiding meat prevents excess weight. Determining whether the diets themselves explain the pattern would require direct measurements of food consumption, calorie intake, and body condition over time.
Stronger Evidence and Complete Nutrition Matter
Knight said the findings provide a reason for further investigation, rather than a definitive answer about vegan diets and feline weight.
“We can’t conclude from this study that vegan diets definitely protect cats against becoming overweight, but we have found a consistent pattern that is worth further investigation. An ideal next step would be a larger, prospective study that directly measured what cats are eating, their energy intake, and their body condition.”
“Additionally, cat carers should always ensure their cats receive nutritionally complete diets, choosing commercial vegan foods that are appropriately supplemented to provide all essential nutrients.”
Reference: “Impacts of a vegan diet on body weight and related health disorders in 1,305 cats: an exploratory cross-sectional survey” by Andrew Knight, Alexander Bauer and Jenny L. Mace, 11 September 2026,

title: A Nutrient Found in Red Meat Could Make Dangerous Inflammation Even Worse
content:
L-carnitine is a naturally occurring compound that helps the body convert fat into energy by transporting fatty acids into mitochondria. Found in high concentrations in skeletal muscle and in foods such as red meat, it is also commonly used in exercise and weight-loss supplements. Credit: Shutterstock
A nutrient known for helping the body burn fat may also cause inflammation when the immune system is in overdrive.
researchers found that L-carnitine, a nutrient abundant in red meat and widely used in exercise and weight-loss supplements, could worsen severe inflammation in mice. After a bacterial component triggered inflammation and sharply lowered blood levels of L-carnitine, restoring the nutrient made the animals sicker, suggesting the decline was protective.
The findings were published October 19 in
L-carnitine is best known for helping cells turn fat into energy. The body produces it naturally, and skeletal muscle contains particularly high concentrations.
“L-carnitine helps transport fats into mitochondria so they can be broken down for energy,” says Eric Elliott, MD, PhD, assistant professor of medicine (infectious diseases) at Yale School of Medicine (YSM) and the study’s first author. “In simpler terms, it has become synonymous with fat burning, which is why it has also gained prominence as an exercise and weight-loss supplement.”
Eric Elliott, MD, PhD. Credit: Yale University
The team was investigating metabolic changes during sepsis, a life-threatening condition in which the body’s response to infection damages its own tissues and organs. Much of that damage can come from uncontrolled inflammation rather than a failure to contain the infection.
“Sepsis is incredibly challenging,” Elliott says. “Patients with sepsis can become critically ill, and among patients with sepsis treated in intensive care units, some studies report mortality rates approaching 40%.”
To model the inflammation associated with sepsis, the researchers exposed mice to lipopolysaccharide (LPS), a bacterial component. When L-carnitine levels in the animals’ blood dropped sharply, the team tested whether restoring the nutrient would improve their outcomes.
Replacing the Nutrient Made Things Worse
“We predicted giving carnitine back to these animals might improve their outcomes, but they actually did much worse,” Elliott says. “That told us the reduction in carnitine was an adaptive response.”
To understand why, the researchers conducted experiments in mouse and human immune cells. They found that L-carnitine activated part of the cell’s internal alarm system called the pyrin inflammasome. This triggered an inflammatory response involving the immune signaling molecule IL-17 and increased deaths among the mice.
“What was particularly striking was how detrimental IL-17 was in this model,” Elliott says. The team now wants to investigate whether blocking IL-17 might eventually help a subset of patients with sepsis, although that possibility remains untested.
The findings offer a potential research direction in a field where treatment advances have been limited. “We have made frustratingly little progress in improving sepsis treatment beyond learning how to better deliver fluids, antibiotics, and medications that support blood pressure,” Elliott says.
Damaged Muscle May Fuel Inflammation
Because skeletal muscle contains high levels of L-carnitine, the researchers suspected that its release from damaged muscle could help drive inflammation. Senior author Andrew Wang, MD, PhD, associate professor of medicine (rheumatology, allergy & immunology) and of immunobiology at YSM, says the pathway may have implications beyond sepsis.
Andrew Wang, MD, PhD. Credit: Yale University
“There is tantalizing genetic evidence that the pathway we uncovered could be contributing to inflammation in a variety of diseases, particularly diseases in which muscle involvement has perhaps been thought to be a casualty of the disease rather than a potential driver,” Wang says.
The team found support for this idea in rhabdomyolysis, a condition in which skeletal muscle rapidly breaks down and releases its contents into the bloodstream, potentially causing acute kidney injury. In a mouse model, L-carnitine transport and pyrin inflammasome activation contributed to inflammation, suggesting that immune cells may interpret L-carnitine released from damaged muscle as a warning signal.
The pathway could also be relevant to cardiovascular disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and cancer. Further research is needed to determine whether it contributes to these chronic inflammatory conditions.
What the Findings Mean for Diet
People who eat meat get most of their L-carnitine from food. Vegetarians and vegans tend to make more of it within their bodies, but their overall levels remain lower. The study examined L-carnitine on its own, so the findings do not directly show how eating red meat or taking supplements affects inflammation.
“We did not study red meat as a whole, and carnitine by itself did not induce inflammation,” Elliott says. “A substantial background of inflammation was required, and we do not yet know what inflammatory context might produce this effect in people. We cannot say that carnitine supplementation or heavy red meat consumption is always harmful. It is probably safe most of the time, but there may be specific circumstances in which it becomes a problem.”
Understanding those circumstances is a priority for the team. The researchers want to learn how individual food components interact with a person’s underlying health and inflammatory state and why the same nutrient might have different effects under different conditions.
“Food science currently exists in the realm of phenomenology,” Wang says. “I think that a deep understanding of all the elements that make up food, akin to a periodic table, will be required to understand what makes a ‘good’ or ‘bad’ diet for a particular individual in a particular health state.”

title: New X-Ray Technology Captures 4.6 Times More Light Without Losing Sharpness
content:
Researchers have developed a photonic crystal scintillator by using Marangoni effect-driven interfacial self-assembly to form a monolayer of polystyrene nanospheres on a GAGG:Ce scintillator wafer. Credit:
Dr. Yao Zhu from Chongqing University
Scientists have developed a new approach to X-ray imaging that captures significantly more light without sacrificing image sharpness.
A major obstacle to sharper X-ray images is that much of the light generated inside detectors never reaches the camera. Researchers have developed a nanostructured surface that increased average light output by 4.64 times and improved the imaging signal-to-noise ratio by 13 decibels. The experimental system also maintained spatial resolution finer than 25 μm (about 0.001 inch).
Developed by scientists at Chongqing University, the 26th Institute of CETC, and Stevens Institute of Technology, the approach could help X-ray detectors produce clearer images when very few photons are available. Potential applications include medical scans using lower radiation doses, security screening, and detailed industrial inspections.
Why X-Ray Detectors Trap Their Own Light
X-ray imaging relies on materials called scintillators to convert invisible X-ray radiation into visible light. These “photosensitive” components act as a “translator,” converting the “language” of high-energy radiation into optical signals that cameras or photodetectors can capture and turn into images.
High-density inorganic scintillators (such as GAGG) are particularly effective at absorbing X-rays and generating light, but much of that light cannot escape. Because these materials have a substantially higher refractive index than their surroundings, light striking the surface at certain angles undergoes total internal reflection. Up to 90% of the generated photons can become trapped in guided optical modes, reducing the amount of light available for imaging.
This problem becomes more severe when detectors operate with weak X-ray signals. Increasing scintillator thickness can improve X-ray absorption, but it also allows light to spread sideways before detection, reducing image sharpness. Thinner scintillators preserve fine details but can produce weaker signals.
Researchers demonstrated enhanced X-ray imaging performance with improved light output and signal-to-noise ratio while maintaining high spatial resolution. Credit:
Dr. Yao Zhu from Chongqing University
Using Photonic Crystals to Release Trapped Light
The researchers addressed this trade-off by modifying how light escapes the scintillator rather than increasing its thickness. Their design uses a photonic crystal, a regularly repeating nanoscale structure that changes how light travels through a material.
Through a process known as Bragg diffraction, the periodic structure provides additional momentum that allows previously trapped light to escape into free space. This increases the amount of visible light reaching the detector without requiring a thicker scintillator.
Manufacturing such structures over large areas has been difficult. Conventional lithography offers precise patterning but requires costly equipment and complicated processing, particularly on brittle scintillator surfaces. Simpler self-assembly techniques can cover larger areas, but cracks, missing particles, and poorly aligned crystal regions can reduce light extraction and introduce imaging artifacts.
A New Manufacturing Method Driven by Surface Tension
The team developed a self-assembly technique that uses the Marangoni effect, in which differences in surface tension drive liquid movement. By combining ethanol and water, the researchers created surface tension gradients that helped organize polystyrene nanospheres into a highly ordered layer.
Surfactants helped pack the particles more tightly, while a vibration-free drainage process transferred the assembled structure onto a 25 mm (about 0.98 inch) diameter GAGG scintillator wafer. The resulting photonic crystal consisted of a continuous monolayer of nanospheres arranged in a hexagonal close-packed pattern.
The research was led by Associate Professor Feng Peng of Chongqing University, working with Dr. Ding Yuchong of the 26th Institute of CETC and PhD candidate Kaifeng Liu of Stevens Institute of Technology. Their paper was published in
Opto-Electronic Advances
Toward Clearer Images With Less Radiation
The experimental findings demonstrate that modifying the scintillator surface can substantially improve light extraction while preserving fine image details. This approach could be particularly useful in photon-starved conditions, where limited X-ray exposure makes it difficult to distinguish weak signals from background noise.
Further development is still needed before the technology can be widely adopted. Residual structural defects can affect spatial resolution, and the researchers plan to refine the assembly process and investigate compatibility with other scintillator materials.
This study was financially supported by the Natural Science Foundation of Chongqing, China under grant CSTB2025NSCQ-LZX0041, the Development Foundation of 26th Institute of China Electronics Technology Group Corporation under grant K2605ZZ2025002, the Beijing Natural Science Foundation under Grant L242114 and the National Key Research and Development Program of China under Grant 2019YFC0605203.

title: “The Closest Thing to Magic” – Researchers Create an Invisible Pipe That Moves Liquids Through Thin Air
content:
Water running through an ultrasound tube. The water flow is controlled by ultrasound emitted through 256 speakers. Credit: Veikko Somerpuro
Scientists have developed an invisible tube made entirely of ultrasonic waves that can guide liquids through mid-air without physical contact.
Researchers at the
University of Helsinki
have created a pipe with no physical walls, using ultrasound to guide a stream of liquid horizontally through open air. The technology could provide a new way to transport corrosive, sticky, or contamination-sensitive substances without exposing them to the surfaces of conventional pipes.
“Of all the experimental setups I have seen, I would say this is the closest thing to magic,” says Ari Salmi, Professor of Electronics at the University of Helsinki, who led the development of the device.
How Ultrasound Creates an Invisible Pipe
The system uses 256 miniature speakers arranged in a cylinder around the flowing liquid, approximately five centimeters (2 inches) away. They produce ultrasonic waves at a frequency of about 40 kilohertz, beyond the range of human hearing. By carefully coordinating these waves, the researchers create an acoustic field that confines the liquid to a narrow path without any solid walls.
Unlike conventional piping, the ultrasonic channel can change direction without requiring physical adjustments. Researchers can electronically reshape the path, redirect the liquid toward another destination, or control its release with single-drop precision. “By changing how the speakers are controlled, we can reshape and turn the tube as needed,” explains postdoctoral researcher Dmitry Nikolaev, who led the project team.
https://youtu.be/qmslDZWmiaE
Video material of the ultrasound tube transmitting liquids, powder, mist and electricity. Taken from the article Contactless continuous guidance of matter in its main states using curved elongated Bessel-like acoustic fields. Credit: Dmitry Nikolaev
The approach can also be adapted for different materials. “Transporting a solid substance, for example, requires a different field configuration than transporting a liquid or a gas.” Beyond moving matter, the ultrasonic tube can guide an electrical discharge along a controlled route.
Salmi first conceived the idea four years ago, following earlier research into using ultrasound to clean the inside of pipes. “We had been developing a device that cleaned the inner surfaces of pipes with ultrasound. At a lunch with a colleague, we discussed that it would be handy if a pipe had no surface for dirt to stick to.”
The discussion stayed with him. During an evening walk with his dog, he realized that ultrasound might be used to form the walls of a pipe rather than simply clean them. Turning the concept into a functioning device required extensive experimentation to determine how the speakers should operate together. The University of Helsinki researchers worked with collaborators at the Public University of Navarre and the University of Michigan to develop the system.
A Small Prototype With Potential for Expansion
The completed prototype produces an ultrasonic tube just eight centimeters (3.1 inches) long, shorter than the diameter of the surrounding device. Nikolaev says multiple modules could be connected to extend the channel to greater lengths. Each eight-centimeter section consumes approximately 50 watts of electricity, comparable to a traditional incandescent light bulb.
Although the device operates beyond human hearing, its ultrasonic field is extremely intense, and dogs may find the sound unpleasant. “At the core of the device, the intensity of the ultrasound is comparable to a continuous roar of gunfire right next to your ear,” Nikolaev says. “Even right here next to it, the sound could be compared to a jet engine if you were standing right beside it. But it is too high-pitched for the human ear.”

title: Uranus and Neptune May Have Been Cosmic Strangers All Along, New Research Reveals
content:
Uranus, the seventh planet from the Sun, is an ice giant whose atmosphere and chemical composition hold clues to the early history of our solar system. Credit: Shutterstock
Uranus and Neptune have long been considered planetary twins, but new research suggests their similarities may conceal surprisingly different origins.
Neptune may have formed from material that originated much closer to the young Sun, challenging the long-standing belief that it and Uranus developed from the same reservoir of cosmic ingredients. New research suggests the two ice giants, despite their striking similarities, have significantly different chemical histories.
An international research team, including scientists from Southwest Research Institute (SwRI), found evidence that Neptune’s deep atmosphere contains substantially more oxygen than Uranus’s. Published in the September 2026 issue of
Astronomy & Astrophysics
, the study uses atmospheric observations and computer models to investigate how the planets acquired their chemical compositions roughly 4.5 billion years ago.
Two Similar Planets With Different Chemical Histories
Uranus and Neptune have comparable sizes, masses, and atmospheric conditions, making them appear almost like planetary twins. Neither has a solid surface like Earth. Instead, their atmospheres extend thousands of miles into their interiors, with water, ammonia, and methane among the compounds present. Methane in their upper atmospheres helps produce their distinctive blue-green colors by absorbing red wavelengths of sunlight.
“Uranus and Neptune may resemble twins today, but their chemistry is telling us that they are more like cousins with very different histories,” said Dr. Olivier Mousis, a program director in SwRI’s Solar System Science and Exploration Division in Boulder, Colorado, and a co-author of the study. “Their atmospheric compositions may be connected to different regions of the protoplanetary disk where the planets formed, which would make their similarities a noteworthy coincidence.”
The scientific community has traditionally considered the ice giants Neptune and Uranus as twins that pulled from the same reservoir of materials when forming. A Southwest Research Institute scientist contributed to a new study detailing how Neptune’s deep atmosphere appears substantially richer in oxygen than Uranus’s, hinting that the materials that make up the two planets came from different regions in the protoplanetary disk. Pictured: an artist’s rendition of Uranus, Neptune, the young Sun and the protoplanetary disk. Credit: Southwest Research Institute
Carbon Monoxide Offers a Window Into Hidden Atmospheres
To investigate the planets’ chemical differences, researchers analyzed carbon monoxide measurements, including recent observations from the Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA). Although scientists cannot directly sample the deep atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune, carbon monoxide concentrations in their upper atmospheres can help constrain the chemistry of the layers below.
The team combined these observations with atmospheric chemistry models to estimate oxygen abundances and carbon-to-oxygen ratios. Their results indicate that Neptune’s deeper atmosphere is considerably more oxygen-rich than Uranus’s, suggesting that the two planets incorporated different proportions of carbon-bearing and oxygen-bearing materials during formation.
“We can’t directly access the deep atmospheres of Uranus and Neptune, but chemical tracers allow us to probe the conditions hidden beneath their visible clouds,” Mousis said. “Studying carbon monoxide, or CO, is particularly useful because of its abundance in the upper troposphere. Using this data, we can model the chemical evolution of the protoplanetary disk and the origins of its materials.”
Neptune’s Building Blocks May Have Traveled Across the Early Solar System
The researchers then examined how these chemical differences could have developed within the protoplanetary disk, the rotating collection of gas and dust surrounding the young Sun. As the disk cooled, volatile compounds condensed into solids at different temperatures and distances. This process created reservoirs of material with distinct chemical compositions, providing different ingredients for growing planets.
“Neptune’s chemistry is difficult to reconcile with the idea that it formed where we see it today, pulling from the same reservoir of cosmic materials as Uranus,” Mousis said. “Instead, our models lead us to believe that its building blocks traveled a long way to where Neptune could accrete them. In short, two superficially similar worlds may have reached their present locations and formations through two very distinct evolutionary paths.”
What Future Missions Could Reveal
The proposed formation scenario remains dependent on atmospheric and planetary formation models. Without direct measurements from deep within Uranus and Neptune, scientists cannot fully determine their internal compositions or reconstruct the movement of materials that shaped them. Future spacecraft observations and atmospheric probes could provide more precise constraints on their chemistry and formation histories.
“Our findings have implications beyond Neptune and Uranus and even far beyond our Solar System,” Mousis said. “Planets comparable in size to Uranus and Neptune are common around other stars, which is why Uranus and Neptune are essential benchmarks for understanding how planets form and evolve throughout the galaxy, and it is precisely why missions like NASA’s planned Uranus Orbiter and Probe, expected to launch sometime in the next decade, are so important.”
Reference: “Contrasting C/O ratios in Uranus and Neptune from disequilibrium chemistry: A clue to distinct evolutionary pathways?” by T. Briand, V. Hue, O. Mousis, T. Cavalié, T. Benest Couzinou, A. Schneeberger and M. D. Hofstadter, 19 October 2026,
Astronomy & Astrophysics

title: Scientists Discover How Dead Stars Could Break One of Physics’ Most Famous Limits
content:
White dwarfs are the small, incredibly dense remnants left behind when stars like our Sun exhaust their nuclear fuel and shed their outer layers. Roughly the size of Earth, these stellar cores can contain a mass comparable to that of the Sun. Credit: Shutterstock
New simulations suggest that powerful internal magnetic fields could allow some white dwarfs to grow far beyond a long-established stellar mass limit.
New research suggests that some white dwarfs, the incredibly dense remnants of dead stars, could grow far heavier than a fundamental limit in astrophysics predicts. Computer simulations show that powerful internal magnetic fields may allow these objects to reach about 2.4 times the Sun’s mass, well beyond the conventional limit of roughly 1.4 solar masses.
The findings, published in
The Astrophysical Journal Letters
, offer a possible explanation for unusually bright stellar explosions and could have implications for how astronomers measure the expansion of the universe. They also demonstrate a potential evolutionary path through which these exceptionally massive stars could form.
How Magnetic Fields Could Overcome a Stellar Mass Limit
White dwarfs form when stars exhaust their nuclear fuel and lose their outer layers, leaving behind compact cores typically about the size of Earth. Despite their small dimensions, these remnants can contain a substantial fraction of the Sun’s mass. For white dwarfs without strong magnetic fields or rapid rotation, the maximum stable mass is approximately 1.4 solar masses, a threshold known as the Chandrasekhar limit.
Researchers at the Department of Physics, Indian Institute of Science (IISc), and their collaborators found that strong magnetic fields could change this restriction. As a white dwarf draws material from a companion star, its increasing mass causes it to become denser and contract. This compression strengthens its internal magnetic field, generating additional pressure that helps counteract gravity and allows the star to support more mass than conventional models predict.
Banibrata Mukhopadhyay (left) and Zenia Zuraiq (right) Credit: Photo: Mriganka Dutta Supernova Image: X-ray: NASA/CXC/U.Texas/S.Post et al; Infrared: 2MASS/UMass/IPAC-Caltech/NASA/NSF
The simulations also suggest that magnetic fields can alter the relationship between a white dwarf’s mass and radius. This effect could help explain observations of certain low-mass white dwarfs that appear larger than expected.
Simulating the Evolution of an Exceptionally Massive White Dwarf
To investigate whether such objects could actually develop through stellar evolution, the scientists modified STARS, a computer program developed at the University of Cambridge. They incorporated the effects of magnetic fields and white dwarf cooling, allowing them to follow a star from its main-sequence phase, when hydrogen fusion powers its core, through its transformation into a white dwarf. They then modeled how the remnant would evolve as it accumulated material from a companion star.
In one simulation, a star initially eight times the Sun’s mass produced a carbon-oxygen white dwarf weighing approximately 1.02 solar masses. When the remnant gained material at a rate of 10⁻⁹ solar masses per year, its magnetic field strengthened enough to support a modeled mass limit of approximately 2.4 solar masses. Under comparable conditions without magnetic effects, the limit remained near 1.4 solar masses.
“The important question was not simply whether a super-Chandrasekhar white dwarf is possible, but whether a star can actually evolve into one,” says Zenia Zuraiq, first author of the study and PhD student at the Department of Physics. “Our simulations allowed us to follow that evolutionary pathway from the main-sequence star to the white dwarf, and show that under certain conditions, such a pathway is possible.”
A Longstanding Theory Gains Support From Simulations
The possibility of white dwarfs exceeding the Chandrasekhar limit has been explored theoretically for decades. Astronomers have also observed unusually luminous Type Ia supernovae, raising the possibility that some originate from white dwarfs substantially more massive than expected. Previous interpretations have suggested progenitor masses, and possible upper limits, approaching 2.8 times the Sun’s mass.
The new study builds on an investigation that began more than a decade ago. “The idea started in 2011, when a summer student came to me and I gave him a problem quite casually: to check whether the Chandrasekhar limit can be violated by a magnetic field,” explains Banibrata Mukhopadhyay, Professor at the Department of Physics and corresponding author of the study published in
The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
Unlike calculations that examine whether an unusually massive white dwarf could remain stable, the new simulations follow the process by which such a remnant might develop. The results support the theoretical possibility of magnetically sustained white dwarfs, although they do not establish how commonly these objects occur in nature.
Possible Implications for Measuring the Expanding Universe
Type Ia supernovae can occur when carbon-oxygen white dwarfs undergo runaway thermonuclear burning. As a white dwarf approaches the Chandrasekhar limit, conditions in its interior can become extreme enough to ignite carbon and potentially trigger a catastrophic explosion.
Astronomers use Type Ia supernovae as standardizable candles to estimate distances across the universe. Although their intrinsic brightness varies, relationships between their luminosity and how their light changes over time allow scientists to calibrate these explosions. Such measurements have played a central role in understanding cosmic expansion.
If some Type Ia supernovae originate from unusually massive, strongly magnetized white dwarfs, differences in their progenitors could influence the properties and brightness of their explosions. Understanding those effects may help astronomers interpret exceptionally luminous supernovae and improve the physical models underlying cosmic distance measurements.
Reference: “Super-Chandrasekhar White Dwarfs by the Evolution of Magnetized Main-sequence Stars: New Mass Limits from STARS Simulation” by Zenia Zuraiq, Banibrata Mukhopadhyay, Achal Kumar, Arnab Sarkar, Alexander J. Hackett, Projjwal Banerjee and Christopher A. Tout, 8 October 2026,
The Astrophysical Journal Letters

title: Alzheimer’s-Linked Proteins Have a Hidden Role in Human Reproduction
content:
Amyloids are proteins that assemble into tightly packed, highly stable fibers. Although best known for their association with neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s, amyloids can also perform useful biological functions. Credit: Stock
Proteins commonly associated with devastating brain diseases may have an unexpected role in reproduction.
Proteins commonly associated with Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease may have a surprising function in human reproduction. Researchers at Columbia University’s Zuckerman Institute have discovered that amyloid fibrils, tiny protein fibers found in semen, can help transport RNA into sperm cells. The findings suggest a previously unknown pathway for moving genetic material into sperm and could eventually lead to new methods for delivering gene therapies.
The investigation grew out of earlier research showing that amyloid fibrils in semen can help HIV enter cells in the reproductive tract. Anthony Fitzpatrick, PhD, a Columbia researcher who studies amyloids in brain diseases, wondered whether these same structures might help transport the body’s own genetic material into sperm.
His team focused on RNA, a molecule involved in converting genetic instructions into proteins and regulating gene activity. Seminal fluid contains numerous small RNA molecules that may influence gene expression during embryonic development. However, scientists have not fully understood how these molecules move from semen into sperm.
HIV provided a potential connection because the virus uses RNA as its genetic material. If seminal amyloids could facilitate viral entry into cells, researchers reasoned, they might also help deliver free RNA molecules.
William Mallen, PhD, the study’s lead author, investigated whether amyloid fibrils could attach to RNA. The two have complementary electrical properties: amyloids carry a positive charge, while RNA is negatively charged. Using fluorescent markers, Mallen confirmed that the molecules bind together.
Fibrils (yellow) inside a sperm cell. Credit: William Mallen / Fitzpatrick lab / Columbia’s Zuckerman Institute
The researchers proposed that amyloids might also protect RNA during transport. RNA is relatively fragile and can be broken down by enzymes, whereas amyloid fibrils form highly stable structures. Encasing RNA within these fibers could potentially help preserve it, although that protective function has not yet been established.
To determine whether the fibrils actually enter sperm, the team used cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), a powerful imaging technique that creates detailed three-dimensional views of frozen biological samples. Amyloid fibers marked with tiny gold particles were found inside sperm cells, confirming that they could cross the cell boundary rather than simply attach to its surface.
“Seeing those amyloid fibers inside sperm cells was just so extraordinary to me,” said Mallen, who is now a medical student at the University of Vermont. “There were hints of this happening earlier in our other experiments, but actually seeing this just totally blew us away.”
Additional experiments using fluorescent markers showed that amyloid fibrils greatly increased the amount of RNA entering sperm. The researchers also identified a possible mechanism for releasing the transported material: a protein called clusterin could help separate RNA from its amyloid carrier once inside cells.
The team tested whether the fibrils could deliver larger RNA molecules capable of directing protein production. Sperm exposed to amyloid-bound RNA encoding green fluorescent protein were used in fertilization experiments. The resulting embryos produced at least 10 times more of the fluorescent protein than embryos fertilized with sperm exposed to the same RNA without amyloids.
Previous studies have suggested that RNA carried by sperm can influence gene activity in offspring through epigenetic mechanisms, which regulate how genes are used without altering the underlying DNA sequence. Research in mice has also linked paternal transmission of certain metabolic conditions, including insulin resistance, to RNA-mediated processes.
Beyond reproduction, the findings could have implications for RNA delivery in medicine. Technologies such as CRISPR rely on RNA to guide gene-editing machinery toward specific DNA sequences, but getting these components safely and efficiently into cells remains a major challenge.
Some gene therapies use modified viruses to transport genetic material into cells. Although effective in many applications, viral delivery systems can provoke immune responses. Amyloid fibrils derived from human proteins might eventually provide another approach, although their safety and effectiveness as therapeutic carriers still require investigation.
“Since the amyloid fibrils we looked at are human-based, hopefully the immune system won’t react in the same way they do to the repurposed viruses often used in gene therapy,” Mallen said.
Reference: “Amyloid-mediated RNA uptake by sperm for embryonic delivery” by William S. title: New additive slows crystallization to push evaporated perovskite LED efficiency to 25%
content:
New additive slows crystallization to push evaporated perovskite LED efficiency to 25%
Researchers at Nanjing University, Nanjing Tech University, Northwestern Polytechnical University, Linköping University, Changzhou University and the Shanghai Synchrotron Radiation Facility have developed a way to control crystallization in thermally evaporated perovskite films, enabling near-infrared perovskite LEDs (PeLEDs) with a record-class external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 25.0%.
(a) In situ monitoring setup used to reveal rapid crystallization and phase evolution in evaporated perovskites. (b) A PyDA-mediated hydrogen-bonding network suppresses premature perovskite formation and regulates crystallization during annealing. (c) The optimized near-infrared PeLED achieves a peak EQE of 25.0%. (d,e) Monolithic integration of dual-wavelength PeLED pixels emitting at 805 and 759 nm. Image credit: Nanjing University
Thermal evaporation is attractive for PeLED manufacturing because it is scalable and allows high-resolution pixel patterning, as in OLED production. But evaporated PeLEDs have long trailed solution-processed ones in efficiency. Without solvents to guide the process, the perovskite crystallizes too fast and too early during vacuum deposition. Using in situ optical spectroscopy and grazing-incidence wide-angle X-ray scattering, the team tracked how evaporated films crystallize and found that the 3D perovskite phase forms prematurely during deposition, followed by distinct crystallization stages during annealing.
To address this, the researchers added a dual-amide molecule, 2,6-pyridine dicarboxamide (PyDA), to the evaporation process. PyDA forms a hydrogen-bond network with formamidinium iodide that stops the 3D perovskite from forming during deposition and then releases the formamidinium gradually during annealing. The 3D phase takes about 420 seconds to form, almost seven times longer than with 5-aminovaleric acid, an additive that works well in solution-processed PeLEDs but does little in evaporated films.
The slower crystallization makes a large difference to film quality. The photoluminescence quantum efficiency rose from 12.6% in the control film to 82.4%, and the photoluminescence lifetime grew from 214 ns to 809 ns. The team says defect-related non-radiative recombination fell by about an order of magnitude.
The resulting devices emit at 805 nm and reach a peak EQE of 25.0% (22.1% on average), with a turn-on voltage of 1.3 V. The operational half-life (T50) is 23 hours at a current density of 100 mA/cm². The team says this is one of the highest EQEs reported for evaporated perovskite emitters and competitive with leading solution-processed devices. The films are also uniform over large areas: devices across a 10 x 10 cm² film consistently exceeded 20% EQE, and the team also made a 5 x 5 cm² device.
To show the advantage for pixelation, the researchers made mixed-halide devices emitting between 748 and 771 nm, with peak EQEs of 12.9% to 17.3%, and integrated two emission wavelengths (805 nm and 759 nm) on a single substrate. They used the dual-wavelength pixel to build a wearable-style pulse oximeter, which measured blood oxygen saturation within 0.95% (mean absolute deviation) of a commercial oximeter.

title: Meta Built Humanoid Prototype With Chinese Startup To Ramp Up Robotics Push
content: Meta Platforms has built a prototype humanoid with Chinese robotics company Fourier and is already working on a second version, as the social media giant steps up efforts to develop robots for people’s homes, according to people familiar with the initiative. Meta and Fourier built the roughly 106-pound humanoid, known internally as Max, in just three months. The goal was to help Meta develop a more polished future product at its robotics arm that it could eventually release as a product, one of the people said, adding that no launch target had been set. While it’s still a relatively early step, the prototype represents the most concrete progress in Meta’s robotics aspirations since it launched Meta Robotics Studio early last year and tapped the former chief executive of General Motors’ autonomous vehicle unit, Cruise, to run it. Meta has also focused on the software side of robotics, in May acquiring Assured Robot Intelligence , a startup that developed AI models for training robots to understand and adapt to human behavior in different environments. Meta’s ambition to develop consumer robots that can help with housework and everyday tasks has taken on new urgency with the launch of the company’s consumer-focused AI agent, Muse. Chief Technology Officer Andrew Bosworth has described humanoid robots internally as a physical embodiment of Muse, the knowledgeable people said. Building Max required Meta’s team to travel to China to work closely with Fourier. Meta’s vice president of product for robotics, Li-Chen Miller, spent almost two months at Fourier’s factory in Shanghai to collaborate on the prototype, two of the people said. That trip culminated in an in-person demonstration of Max to some employees at the end of August as part of an internal robotics summit, those people said. The partnership comes as the Trump administration has stepped up scrutiny of China’s robotics sector—which dominates global production—and raised questions about the national security implications of U.S. companies relying on Chinese firms for parts. In July, the Federal Communications Commission barred imports of new models of Chinese humanoid robots, citing potential supply chain and cybersecurity risks. Under existing FCC import rules, companies can import up to 4,000 units of devices for testing or product development, provided they are not marketed or sold. That exemption allows U.S. companies including Meta to bring in prototypes from China for research and development purposes. But in August the FCC proposed lowering that threshold to just 40 units for devices covered by its restrictions, unless companies obtain written approval from the agency to import more. The proposal could make it harder for Meta and other companies to bring batches of prototypes into the U.S. for testing and development, and difficult to obtain a steady supply of parts to build robots for sale. A spokesperson for Meta said: “We face the same realities as the rest of the industry when it comes to sourcing components that are not readily available domestically. However, this effort with Fourier is focused on internal research and experimentation, and we have no plans to sell these units.” Stiff Competition in Humanoid Robotics If Meta does end up trying to sell humanoids to consumers, it would face stiff competition. Chinese companies are already producing such robots at scale, and Elon Musk is heavily betting the future of his electric vehicle company, Tesla, on its Optimus humanoid robot, now in its third version. In addition, prominent startups including Figure and 1X Technologies have been working on humanoids for years. Despite the buzz surrounding humanoids, consumer adoption within homes is still in its early days. Figure has begun testing its robots in home environments, while 1X has started taking pre-orders for its NEO robots. The Meta robotics division has recently undergone a leadership change. Meta tapped Ning Li to serve as interim leader of Meta Robotics Studio after Marc Whitten, the former Cruise CEO, left the company at the end of August, just 18 months after joining, according to two people familiar with the matter. Li reports to Bosworth, who has taken over Whitten’s former responsibilities and has been closely involved in Meta Robotics Studio, one person said. Bosworth has held regular meetings with the team and spent time digging into the division’s technical and operational challenges, the person said. Max, which stands about 1.5 meters tall, or just under 5 feet, is currently powered by Nvidia’s Jetson Thor chip and a separate software platform that helps it move. It has two speakers built into its chest, and the eyes and mouth on its face can mimic human expressions. Its five-fingered hands can pick up small bottles and toys. Meta built its custom robot using Fourier’s hardware and insights from the first, second and third generations of its series of robots. The companies then increased the prototype’s height, changed its proportions and altered its head design, display and cameras, while adding hands and shoes. Meta also laid out specific requirements for how the robot should perceive and respond to people in a home environment. The two companies designed Max based on several requirements from Meta, including the ability to recognize a voice from 5 meters away, interpret a hand gesture or wave from 3 meters away, hold eye contact, and signal various states such as listening, thinking, speaking and uncertainty. Meta and Fourier started building Max 2 in September. It will include a redesigned torso and reworked hands with better manipulation skills, as well as a projector to display visual content, the people said. It will also have additional sensors to help it go up and down stairs. Meta is also building out the team it may need to eventually manufacture robots in large numbers. The company is looking to hire a supplier development engineer in Shanghai to work with product design and manufacturing and help scale robotics “from prototype through mass production,” according to a job posting viewed by The Information. Meta is also hiring a product design engineer and a technical program manager for Meta Robotics Studio in Shenzhen, China, to oversee prototype development, planning and mass production, according to two other job postings.

title: 科学网-第八届华夏肿瘤论坛在北京开幕
content:
第八届华夏肿瘤论坛在北京开幕
10月30-31日，第八届华夏肿瘤论坛暨中国医疗保健国际交流促进会肝脏肿瘤学分会2026年年会在北京开幕。大会由中国医疗保健国际交流促进会肝脏肿瘤学分会主办，国家癌症中心、中国医学科学院肿瘤医院承办，中国医疗保健国际交流促进会神经内分泌肿瘤学分会、放射肿瘤学分会、消化肿瘤综合治疗学分会、肿瘤免疫治疗学分会、软组织肿瘤学分会及《肝癌电子杂志》共同协办。
会议现场（主办方供图）
肿瘤防治关系人民群众生命健康，是推进健康中国建设的重要任务。落实全国卫生与健康大会精神，需要将预防为主、规范诊疗、科技创新与全程管理更加紧密地结合起来，推动防治关口前移，促进研究成果向临床应用转化。在此背景下，本届论坛以“规范、仁心、传承、发展”为主题，聚焦精准医疗、免疫治疗、人工智能、早期筛查与预防、转化医学等方向，汇聚肿瘤防治领域专家学者，共同探讨提升肿瘤综合防治能力的实践路径。
来自各省级癌症中心、省市级肿瘤医院、综合医院以及肿瘤防治领域的知名专家学者参加大会。大会主席、中国医学科学院肿瘤医院蔡建强教授致欢迎辞。中国医学科学院肿瘤医院毕新宇教授主持开幕式。
中国医疗保健国际交流促进会副会长兼秘书长翟晓辉表示，医促会将一如既往地支持分会工作，希望新一届委员会传承创新、继续发展，在既有工作基础上推动分会建设与学术交流不断迈上新台阶。
大会主席、中国医学科学院肿瘤医院蔡建强教授指出，我国肿瘤防治事业正经历从以疾病为中心向以人民健康为中心的深刻转变，肿瘤防治工作的使命已经超越单纯的治病，延伸到涵盖预防、筛查、诊疗、康复的全链条系统工程。面向“十五五”这一关键时期，应主动融入健康中国建设大局，把全链条、全病程的健康服务做实做细，更好回应人民群众的健康需求。
中国科学院院士滕皋军教授代表中国医师协会介入医师分会向第八届华夏肿瘤论坛的召开表示热烈祝贺。他表示，介入医学界愿与各兄弟学会和广大同道携手，在规范诊疗、人才培养与临床研究等方面持续深化合作，以更加紧密的学科协同提升肿瘤综合防治水平，为健康中国建设贡献力量。
开幕式后举行大咖讲坛。中国科学院院士蔡秀军、中国工程院院士于金明、中国科学院院士樊嘉以及北京化工大学卢云峰教授、中国医学科学院肿瘤医院蔡建强教授先后作主题报告，分别围绕“原创性研究的方法路径”“2026肿瘤治疗十大进展”“肝胆肿瘤的创新实践”“病灶自主导航药物”“肝癌精准系统治疗体系的建立”等议题展开阐述。
此外，本届大会还围绕肿瘤防治前沿与临床需求，设置了肝脏肿瘤学分会2026年年会、2026华夏肿瘤免疫治疗进展论坛、2026华夏神经内分泌肿瘤论坛、华夏消化肿瘤精准治疗论坛、华夏软组织肿瘤论坛等专题学术活动。
